description: Part evals for desktop-distribution in the skill-creator schema, plus checks: the rule ids of rules.json each case exercises. Each expectation starts with a bracketed tag, a rule id or a short name. Each case runs with and without the apple skill on Claude Code and Codex; files are copied into the root of an empty project first.

evals.name: helper-other-team
evals.prompt: Our Mac app Relay starts a helper described in Relay.app/Contents/Resources/helper.json, and the app's listener refuses it (see logs/relay.log). codesign-node.txt is what codesign printed for the node it runs. The same helper works when I start it by hand. Why is it refused, and what should we change?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the helper runs a node from Homebrew that is not signed by the app's team, so the listener's team check refuses it; the fix is to bundle node inside the app, sign it with the app's Developer ID and start it by its bundled path, then check with probe-app.mjs and the app's log.
expectations: [DD-TEAM-01] It names the cause: the helper starts /opt/homebrew/bin/node, ad hoc signed with no team, while the listener accepts only the app's team.
[fix] It bundles the runtime inside the app, signs it inside out with the app's identity (hardened runtime, timestamp), and changes helper.json to the bundled path.
[verify] It verifies with codesign --verify --deep --strict and the team identifiers (probe-app.mjs or equivalent) and with the app's own log, not only by starting the helper by hand.
[no-guess] It does not loosen the listener's team check to make the helper pass.

evals.name: installer-review
evals.prompt: People install Relay with curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | bash, using install.sh. Review it and fix it so it is safe to publish.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten installer that downloads over https, compares the SHA-256 with a pinned value, verifies the app with codesign --verify --deep --strict, stages it with ditto and swaps it in with two renames, removes quarantine with /usr/bin/xattr only from the verified copy, and registers it with lsregister; checked with check-installer.mjs.
expectations: [DD-INSTALL-01] The download uses https and the archive SHA-256 is compared with a pinned value before unpacking, stopping on a mismatch.
[DD-INSTALL-02] The unpacked app is verified with codesign --verify --deep --strict before it replaces the installed copy.
[DD-INSTALL-03] It no longer deletes the installed app first or copies over it: it stages with ditto and swaps with two renames, restoring the old copy if the swap fails.
[DD-WARN-XATTR] Quarantine is removed with /usr/bin/xattr, after the checks, only from the verified copy.
[check] It runs check-installer.mjs (or makes the same checks) on the result and reports the summary.

evals.name: cask-upgrade
evals.prompt: Our tap has Casks/relay.rb. brew style complains, and after every brew upgrade Relay no longer starts at login. Relay updates itself with Sparkle (Relay/Info.plist). Fix the cask.
evals.expected_output: A cask without the postflight Ruby block, whose uninstall only quits the app while the login item and the Application Support folder move to zap, with auto_updates true; checked with check-cask.mjs --self-updating and brew style --cask.
expectations: [DD-CASK-01] The postflight do ... end block is removed or replaced by the declarative install-step stanza, and it says to confirm the stanza with brew style --cask.
[DD-CASK-02] It explains that brew upgrade runs uninstall, and moves login_item and the ~/Library delete into zap.
[DD-CASK-03] It adds auto_updates true because the app updates itself with Sparkle.
[check] It runs check-cask.mjs --self-updating (or the same checks) and names brew style --cask and brew audit --cask as the authority.

evals.name: feed-first-build
evals.prompt: Users on Apple silicon Macs say Relay never updates past the version they installed, while Intel Macs and Windows update fine. Our release job writes dist/latest.json and runs scripts/check-release.mjs. What is wrong and how do we stop it happening again?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the feed has no darwin-aarch64 entry although the aarch64 archive and signature were built, and that the release check only requires platforms already served, so it can never require the first; the fix adds the entry and changes the gate to require every built platform, checked with check-feed.mjs --platforms.
expectations: [DD-FEED-01] It finds that latest.json lacks darwin-aarch64 while files.txt lists the aarch64 archive and its .sig, and adds the entry with the https url and the signature.
[gate] It changes check-release.mjs to require every platform the job built, not the ones already served, and explains why the served list never gains a platform.
[check] It runs check-feed.mjs with --platforms naming every built platform (or makes the same check).

evals.name: adhoc-download
evals.prompt: We sign our Mac app ad hoc and put the zip on our website. People who download it get a message that it cannot be opened. Should our install page just tell them to use Open Anyway in System Settings?
evals.expected_output: No: a Developer ID build that is notarized and stapled is the way to give a download to other people; an ad hoc build is only for the developer's Macs or a checksum-checking curl installer. It explains quarantine, how to check the result with spctl, and hands notarization to the notarization row.
expectations: [DD-WARN-ADHOC] It does not recommend Open Anyway as the install path and explains that the browser download carries the quarantine flag that Gatekeeper checks.
[DD-GATE-01] It recommends a Developer ID build with the hardened runtime and a timestamp, notarized and stapled, and checking it with spctl --assess (probe-app.mjs).
[routing] It hands submitting to the notary service to the notarization row and asks for explicit approval before any submit.
[alternative] If notarization is not possible yet, it offers the checksum-checking curl installer for people who accept it, and says what that does not protect.
